title: Hey Microsoft, Why Can't You Ever Make Entertainment Work?
body:
## Fifteen years after Gates unveiled "Consumer Electronics Plus," Microsoft is, outside your working hours, a largely invisible B2B company.

Regular article

Last week Microsoft announced it was shutting down Zune, its music service. After nearly nine years, four generations of hardware and several name changes, Microsoft has given up on it.

The closure is only the latest in a string of consumer failures. Last year Microsoft closed Xbox Entertainment Studios, which was meant to make original series, and the Nokia handset business it bought for US$9 billion saw its market share fall below 3%, which is as good as dead. Even the Xbox, which once carried Microsoft's dream of a "living-room entertainment center," has watched its latest console fall behind Sony's PS4.

Microsoft still earns US$20 billion a year, but the money now comes only from office software and cloud computing, businesses that drift ever further from individual users. Nearly every piece of Microsoft news you hear today that touches consumers or entertainment is bad news. Even the Surface Pro tablet sells well mainly because it is bundled with Office and sold to companies.

Today anyone will tell you Microsoft missed smartphones and missed digital entertainment... But in January 2000, when Bill Gates announced the "Consumer Electronics Plus" (Consumer Electronics - Plus) initiative at CES, the international consumer electronics show, nobody dared underestimate his empire.

![In 2001, Gates unveils the Xbox game console at CES](/uploads/image/201509/d74caed87185.jpg)In 2001, Gates unveils the Xbox game console at CES

In 2000 Apple was not yet ready to launch the iPod. It was just a small company making expensive computers, with little to do with consumer electronics. Microsoft, despite the financial crisis, was still worth nearly US$400 billion, the most valuable technology company of its day.

That year 95% of personal computer users ran Windows, but that did not mean the market was saturated.

Microsoft and Intel essentially controlled the PC market between them, and PCs running Windows, Office and an Intel processor had become standard equipment in the modern office.

But as PCs got cheaper and the Netscape browser arrived, the PC could be used for shopping, reading the news, even listening to music and watching video online. It was no longer just an office tool. With that shift, the business's audience grew from a few million companies to billions of consumers.

And the first computing leader to rush into this far larger market was not Jobs, whom people worship today, but Gates.

#### The Xbox Almost Became a PC Stuffed With Games

"If a PC went after games, could it beat Sony's PS2?" In March 1999, after meeting four engineers from DirectX, Microsoft's game-development software, Gates had them spend a quarter looking into it. They urged their big boss to move into games.

Three months later the four came back with two conclusions: the PS2 was the best console on the market, but a PC could easily beat it technically; and making games on PC hardware would not cost that much. Gates finally approved a games business, on one condition: the console had to run Windows.

"We wanted to kill two birds with one stone," recalled Kevin Bachus, one of the four. "We had to build a console, and we couldn't lose the PC games business either." The Xbox nearly turned into a personal computer stuffed with games.

Luckily, Ed Fries, who doubled as the Xbox's first head, did not care much about the project. As Microsoft's vice president of game publishing, he had his hands full dealing with the big game developers.

So J Allard, one of the four, took over the technical side. His staff found him stubborn and hard to get along with, but he persuaded Gates to drop the idea of putting Windows on the Xbox.

![The first-generation Xbox](/uploads/image/201509/6c46570514bf.jpg)The first-generation Xbox

The idea that finally won over his boss was the "digital home": "The TV connects to the game console, to the computer, to everything digital in the home."

Rick Thompson, from Microsoft's hardware division, ran the Xbox. He secured the heart of the console: the graphics chip. The Xbox went on sale in the United States in November 2001. *Halo*, which had attracted little notice during development, became a phenomenon and sold more than 20 million copies worldwide.

The first Xbox made no money at all, but it got Microsoft into a games market dominated by Sony and Nintendo and became Microsoft's first successful consumer electronics product.

### The "Consumer Electronics Plus" Plan: Gates Wanted More Than Games

When Gates launched the "Consumer Electronics Plus" plan in 2000, he promised that besides the Xbox, Microsoft would deliver these products over the next 15 years:

- Phone: Pocket PC, the predecessor of Windows Mobile
- E-book: Microsoft Reader
- Smart home: Microsoft Concept Home
- TV: Microsoft WebTV

Microsoft did build most of them. But it built them the way it built the PC business: write paid software itself, then find partners to make the hardware. The result is that you may never have heard of any of them.

In August 2000 Microsoft teamed up with Barnes & Noble to launch Microsoft Reader. Books in its .LIT format looked good and worked on Windows PCs and handheld computers. The problem was the one that sank every e-book effort before the Kindle: Microsoft had neither enough books nor enough new ones. Users often complained that there were plenty of books but none they wanted to read. E-books finally took off with Amazon's Kindle in 2007.

![The SPOT smartwatch Microsoft built with SUUNTO, 11 years ahead of the Apple Watch](/uploads/image/201509/669b9b50e283.jpg)The SPOT smartwatch Microsoft built with SUUNTO, 11 years ahead of the Apple Watch

The SPOT smartwatch, which Gates and a model wore onto the CES stage in 2003, died because the technology was not ready. MSN Direct, the first smartwatch line, made with watch brands including Fossil, Swatch and SUUNTO, was bulky. With the mobile internet, and even smartphones, not yet widespread, its "smart" features amounted to receiving weather forecasts and stock quotes over radio signals.

#### In Digital Music, Microsoft Lost to Apple Again and Again

Meanwhile Apple, which entered the consumer market later than Microsoft, used the iPod to get closer to users. After 2003 iPod sales exploded, and a big reason was that iTunes came out in a Windows version.

A year later iTunes downloads passed 100 million songs, ten times the earlier figure. Microsoft's angry response was Janus, software modeled on iTunes, and a name for the music service that sounded as if it would sell: PlaysForSure.

Together with Windows Media 10, Microsoft tried to give consumers a simpler service. When it released Janus to music-player makers and websites in mid-2004, it did not realize that it controlled neither the music nor the details of how the hardware was made.

As a result, its partner music sites, PressPlay and MusicNet, let Microsoft down: their sound quality was terrible. And when a music player had a software problem, users could not get quick help from Microsoft's technicians.

PlaysForSure had serious problems of its own. While celebrities were busy recommending the iPod, some of Microsoft's own famous loyalists were complaining about PlaysForSure. The writer Jason Dunn said at the time that the service drove him to despair: it stopped playing for no reason and demanded to be reauthorized, eight to ten times a week.

The iPod kept winning users, and Microsoft fought internally over whether to stay in music at all. One camp wanted to add music features to Windows Mobile phones; the other insisted Microsoft had to make its own hardware and fight the iPod to the end.

The second camp won, and "Project Argo" was born. Its champion was Allard, the Xbox's chief architect, who planned to spend US$500 million on a new music player: the Zune.

![Allard with Gates, each holding a first-generation Zune music player. Allard was involved in a series of Microsoft consumer electronics projects. Image from [Tech Tell](http://www.technologytell.com/gadgets/56691/j-allard-rumored-to-be-leaving-microsoft/)](/uploads/image/201509/29de6f2bb640.jpg)Allard with Gates, each holding a first-generation Zune music player. Allard was involved in a series of Microsoft consumer electronics projects. Image from [Tech Tell](http://www.technologytell.com/gadgets/56691/j-allard-rumored-to-be-leaving-microsoft/)

Consumers did not love the Zune either. After its first Christmas season, Jason Reindorp, Microsoft's head of Zune marketing, declined to give sales figures. A year later NPD data showed the Zune held 2% of the US music-player market.

Allard began to waver, deciding the Zune was only a stepping stone that would supply a cloud music service for the Xbox. At the insistence of Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer, the Zune went through several more generations of players until production stopped in March 2011. The paid subscription service, Zune Music Pass, carried on.

#### The Xbox 360 Became Microsoft's Entertainment Hub, but Microsoft Missed the PC App Store

In the fall of 2009, Zune Music Pass came to the Xbox 360. Back when Allard was building the Zune player, Ballmer would now and then mistakenly call it the Xbox music player.

Just as Allard had once envisioned for the Xbox, the Xbox 360 gradually became Microsoft's entertainment hub. The original Xbox had been dominated by shooters; the Xbox 360's game store offered far more choice. Xbox Live's online multiplayer and cloud saves also drew many users.

For a time the Xbox 360 was the best-selling console in the world, and Ballmer, then CEO, kept pointing to the Kinect motion sensor that followed as proof that the company could still innovate.

By 2007 the PC ran two main kinds of software: expensive office software and games. Everything else hardly mattered; the browser had replaced it all.

Office software was expensive but there was little of it; games were the most varied category of PC software. Riding the Xbox 360's success, Microsoft tried to offer online multiplayer on the PC through Games for Windows - Live. But Games for Windows was not only clumsy to use, it also could not handle the whole process of buying a game, from purchase and download onward.

The service that delivered a seamless gaming experience on the PC was Steam, from the game company Valve. Ironically, many of Valve's core people had once worked at Microsoft.

#### Before Windows Phone: Microsoft's Failures in Mobile

Steam's victory over Games for Windows meant Microsoft had lost its chance to build an attractive software store on the PC. In its phone business, that loss would prove even more costly.

Microsoft was one of the first companies to make phones. PocketPC 2000, the predecessor of Windows Mobile, came out in 2000. Its home screen copied Windows outright, right down to a Start menu.

Then in 2007 Apple released the first iPhone. A new way of interacting through a touchscreen, plus an app store: this was a computer truly designed for the pocket.

Pieter Knook, who ran Windows Mobile, said there was no need to compete with the iPhone, because Microsoft made phones for business. Ballmer answered reporters with his usual salesman's bluster: "It's the most expensive phone in the world ($500). And it doesn't have a keyboard, so it's not a very good email machine."

But it was plain that Windows Mobile's Start menu and toothpick stylus were not the future of the smartphone. Microsoft began preparing a counterattack, but before the chase could begin, the question of who was in charge came up again.

In 2008 Allard launched Project Pink, using Danger, a company Microsoft had acquired, to form the PMX (Premium Mobile Experience) division and design new phones apart from the aging Windows Mobile platform.

Danger had made the popular Sidekick phone, which had the world's first built-in phone app store. Its leader, Andy Rubin, left after the acquisition to build a next-generation mobile operating system, which became Android.

But at the very moment it needed to catch the iPhone, Microsoft's management got tangled up over who should do the catching. The Windows Phone division won, and its head, Andy Lees, seized control of the project.

![The Kin phone, the product of Project Pink](/uploads/image/201509/d16f4e935194.jpg)The Kin phone, the product of Project Pink

Then, to avoid competing with high-end Windows Phone models, the Kin, released in April 2010, came out as two low-end feature phones. By then a new feature-phone system made no sense. The Kin had some bright spots, such as playful interaction design, social network integration and cloud storage that came before iCloud, but it was abandoned less than two months after launch.

That same year Allard's Courier tablet project was also killed. The Courier had two separate screens that could interact with each other, much like the iPad split screen Apple later delivered in iOS 9. But it never got a chance to reach the market. Allard then left Microsoft.

#### Under Its New CEO, Microsoft Has Little Left to Do With Consumers

In 2014 Ballmer retired and became owner of the Clippers. Satya Nadella, a 22-year Microsoft veteran, was promoted to CEO. Before that, Nadella was the man who moved Microsoft to the cloud, including the businesses he had run: Bing search, Office, and servers and cloud computing.

Ballmer once admitted that he went into consumer businesses because he feared Microsoft would become another IBM, forgotten by the public. In Nadella's view, Microsoft was at heart a company built around productivity tools.

Five months into the job, [Nadella cut 18,000 positions](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/1520.html), the biggest layoff in Microsoft's 34 years; 12,500 of them came from the Nokia handset business bought for US$9 billion. After another round of layoffs and restructuring this summer, the phone business no longer matters.

Nor does the Xbox stand outside the Windows world any longer, as its predecessors did. The new Xbox One runs on Windows underneath. And Nadella told *Fortune* that it is no longer a core Microsoft business.

Running Windows and some Windows apps has made the Xbox One bulky and expensive, a big reason its sales disappointed and Sony's PS4 overtook it.

Work software is once again Microsoft's only business. In every quarterly earnings report, the fast-growing businesses Microsoft talks about are Office 365, its online office service, and Azure, its cloud computing business. They are also among the few Microsoft businesses that have kept growing at more than 100% a year over the past several years.

Apart from HoloLens, which is still a long way off, everything you see at a Microsoft launch event today is about work.

Microsoft wants to be "the Sony of the 21st century." So wrote the reporter Jay Greene in 2002, after interviewing Xbox head Robbie Bach.

But 15 years after Gates proposed "Consumer Electronics Plus," outside of work, Microsoft hardly crosses your mind.
